guides.title: Pretraining objective and learned behavior
guides.summary: Pretraining teaches a model to predict patterns in large datasets; useful capabilities emerge from that objective, but product guarantees do not.
guides.mentalModel: Pretraining optimizes a statistical prediction objective over massive sequences. The resulting model internalizes broad patterns and reusable representations, but it is not directly trained to obey your product policy, know current facts or complete one application workflow correctly.
guides.whyItMatters: Understanding the training objective prevents two opposite mistakes: treating a model as a simple database of memorized text, or treating fluent behavior as proof that the model was explicitly trained for your exact task. Pretraining creates a broad capability prior. Instructions, retrieval, tools, validation and post-training shape how that capability is used at runtime, while hard guarantees still belong in application boundaries.

sections.title: From prediction pressure to reusable representations
sections.body: During pretraining, the model repeatedly predicts missing or next pieces of data from context and updates its parameters when predictions are wrong. Across enough diverse examples, those updates reward internal representations that capture syntax, semantics, code patterns, factual associations and many reusable regularities. The objective is broad, so competence can transfer to tasks that were never represented as explicit product requirements.

sections.title: Example: why a base capability still needs an application contract
sections.body: A pretrained model may explain SQL, draft a query and recognize database concepts without having been trained on your production schema or permission rules. An application can exploit that capability by supplying schema context and tools, but authorization, query validation and destructive-action limits must still be enforced outside the model.

failureModes: Assuming pretraining means the model stores a perfectly retrievable copy of its training corpus.
Treating emergent capability as a guarantee of reliable task completion.
Using more prompt text to solve rules that should be enforced by runtime policy.
heuristics: Separate broad model capability from application-specific evidence and guarantees.
Use retrieval or tools for current and private knowledge rather than expecting pretraining to stay current.
Evaluate the exact workload instead of inferring competence from general fluency.
takeaways: Pretraining creates a broad statistical capability base.
Capability does not imply current knowledge, permission or correctness guarantees.
Application architecture determines how pretrained capability becomes reliable product behavior.

practice.title: Decide what belongs at the model layer

guides.title: Parallel agent work
guides.summary: Parallelism helps when subproblems are genuinely independent or provide independent verification; otherwise coordination cost can exceed the speedup.
guides.mentalModel: Parallel agents are concurrent workers over explicitly partitioned state. They earn their complexity when work can proceed independently and their outputs can be reconciled through a clear contract.
guides.whyItMatters: Launching several agents is easy; obtaining trustworthy speedup is not. Agents can duplicate work, edit the same state, propagate inconsistent assumptions or require expensive synthesis. Parallelism should therefore be introduced after decomposition, ownership and merge rules are explicit. Independent verification is often a stronger reason to parallelize than simply creating more personas.

sections.title: Partition work and define the join
sections.body: Identify tasks whose inputs do not depend on one another's intermediate reasoning. Assign each worker a bounded artifact or decision, give it only the relevant context, and define how results will be joined. Shared mutable state should have ownership or serialization rules. The coordinator then verifies completeness, conflicts and evidence quality before accepting the combined result.

sections.title: Example: parallel repository investigation
sections.body: One worker traces an API failure through backend code while another independently inspects frontend request construction. Both return file references, hypotheses and evidence rather than editing the same files immediately. A coordinator compares the findings and assigns one implementation path only after the shared failure boundary is understood.

failureModes: Parallelizing tasks that depend on one another's unresolved intermediate state.
Letting multiple agents write the same files or records without an ownership rule.
Measuring only wall-clock speed while ignoring duplicated tokens, conflicts and synthesis cost.
heuristics: Parallelize independent evidence gathering before parallelizing shared-state mutation.
Give each worker an explicit output contract and ownership boundary.
Measure total coordination cost and defect rate, not just elapsed time.
takeaways: Concurrency is useful only when decomposition is real.
The join step is part of the architecture, not an afterthought.
Independent parallel checks can improve reliability even when they do not reduce latency.

guides.title: Visual briefing for generated media
guides.summary: A strong visual brief turns an aesthetic intention into constraints that can be generated, reviewed and revised consistently.
guides.mentalModel: A visual brief is a production contract for imagery: purpose, audience, composition, subject, style constraints, typography rules, aspect ratio, brand boundaries, references and explicit exclusions.
guides.whyItMatters: Prompts such as 'make it modern' or 'make it beautiful' leave too much room for accidental choices. The model may create attractive output that fails the learning goal, brand system or layout need. A visual brief makes quality inspectable: reviewers can identify whether the problem is composition, hierarchy, subject choice, legibility or style instead of repeatedly regenerating by intuition.

sections.title: Describe the job before the look
sections.body: Start with what the visual must communicate and where it will appear. Specify focal subject, information hierarchy, composition, aspect ratio, text policy, desired realism or abstraction, visual references and things to avoid. Separate invariant brand constraints from variables that may be explored. After generation, review against the brief and change one meaningful dimension at a time.

sections.title: Example: a lesson cover instead of generic AI art
sections.body: A course needs a cover for a lesson about retrieval failure. The brief asks for a simple evidence-selection scene with one stale document visibly competing with a current policy, no humanoid robot, no glowing neural-network background, generous space for the product title and a 16:9 crop. The resulting iterations can be judged against communication and layout requirements, not only taste.

failureModes: Using abstract adjectives without defining composition or communication goals.
Changing subject, style, layout and palette at once after every weak generation.
Putting important text inside generated imagery when exact typography is required.
heuristics: State the communication objective before style descriptors.
Separate non-negotiable constraints from exploratory variables.
Keep exact product copy and critical typography in the UI or design layer when possible.
takeaways: A visual brief makes aesthetic work reviewable.
The image should serve the product job, not merely look impressive.
Controlled iteration produces more reusable visual systems than prompt roulette.

guides.title: Model capability envelope
guides.summary: A model has a workload-dependent envelope of tasks it can perform acceptably; outside that tested envelope, confidence should fall before ambition rises.
guides.mentalModel: Capability is not one scalar score. Think of an envelope across task types, languages, context sizes, tool patterns, modalities, latency budgets and error costs, measured under the harness you actually deploy.
guides.whyItMatters: A model can be excellent at one coding task and unreliable at another, strong in short contexts but unstable in long tool chains, or good on average while failing a high-impact slice. Product design becomes safer when teams know the conditions under which performance has been demonstrated and treat extrapolation outside those conditions as an explicit risk.

sections.title: Map capability by representative slices
sections.body: Define the workload dimensions that matter: task family, difficulty, language, context length, number of tool steps, structured-output demands and consequence of error. Evaluate representative slices under the production harness and record where quality clears the required threshold. The resulting envelope can drive routing, escalation and product scope without pretending that one benchmark predicts every condition.

sections.title: Example: an agent that is reliable only for bounded repository changes
sections.body: A coding model performs well on single-service bug fixes with executable tests but degrades on cross-repository migrations with ambiguous ownership. The product allows autonomous edits inside the tested slice and requires planning plus human review for migrations. The boundary comes from observed capability, not a generic model label.

failureModes: Treating benchmark rank as a universal capability score.
Expanding autonomy to new task classes without evaluating them.
Ignoring how harness, context and tool design change the observed capability.
heuristics: Define capability in terms of workload slices and acceptance thresholds.
Track where evidence is missing as explicitly as where performance is strong.
Re-evaluate the envelope after meaningful model, prompt or tool changes.
takeaways: Capability is conditional on workload and system context.
A tested envelope is more useful than a broad claim that a model is 'smart'.
Autonomy and routing should respect demonstrated capability boundaries.

practice.title: Measure whether adaptation changes the useful envelope

guides.title: Least privilege for AI capabilities
guides.summary: Give an AI system only the permissions required for the current task, for the shortest practical scope, with stronger gates around irreversible effects.
guides.mentalModel: Permission is a runtime capability, not a sentence in the prompt. Least privilege narrows what the system can actually do even when the model is confused, manipulated or simply wrong.
guides.whyItMatters: Prompt instructions can influence model behavior but cannot provide a hard security boundary. If one tool credential can read every customer, delete data and transfer money, a single planning error or prompt-injection path can become a high-impact incident. Narrow scopes, temporary capabilities and action-specific approval reduce the blast radius independently of model intent.

sections.title: Constrain identity, scope and action
sections.body: Map each task to the minimum resources and operations it needs. Issue scoped credentials or capability handles, separate read from write permissions, and keep destructive or high-value operations behind explicit approval or stronger policy checks. Enforce limits in the runtime or external service so a model cannot expand its authority by requesting a different action in natural language.

sections.title: Example: support agent account access
sections.body: A support agent may read the current customer's subscription and issue a small bounded credit. It cannot enumerate all customers, change account ownership or invoke a general payment API. A refund above the threshold requires a separate approved capability. Even if malicious retrieved text asks for broader access, the runtime has no such permission to grant.

failureModes: Giving one broad API key to every agent tool because it is operationally convenient.
Relying on system-prompt warnings instead of permission enforcement.
Keeping elevated capabilities alive after the task that required them is complete.
heuristics: Separate read, write and destructive capabilities wherever practical.
Scope permissions by user, resource, amount and time when the domain supports it.
Treat approval as capability issuance, not merely conversational consent.
takeaways: Least privilege reduces blast radius independently of model quality.
High-impact actions should require narrower and more explicit capabilities.
